findings.claim: Practice question 5 mark scheme: 'AO4 (writer's methods): dialect as characterisation and social commentary.'
findings.truth: On the post-1914 British play question the assessed objectives are AO1, AO3 and AO4, and AO4 is written accuracy: 'Use a range of vocabulary and sentence structures for clarity, purpose and effect, with accurate spelling and punctuation' (8 of the 40 marks). AO2, which covers language, form and structure, is not assessed on this question at all. Analysing Brighouse's methods still earns credit, but through AO1.

findings.claim: Unit-wide (all 7 lessons, 42 questions): every practice question is labelled '40 marks - Post-1914 Essay' but its band ladder runs Top band (21-25) down to Lower band (1-5), i.e. a 25-mark scale.
findings.truth: The question is worth 40 marks (AO1 16 + AO3 16 + AO4 8). A student self-marking against a 25-mark ladder badly misjudges what a top answer is worth. Ladders rescaled across the full 40: 33-40 / 25-32 / 17-24 / 9-16 / 1-8. Band names left as they are, because they are not on the banned list.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md raw-mark table, lines 1310-1400; overview line 1126.

findings.claim: 'In Act 3, Hobson's drinking catches up with him ... He falls through the cellar trapdoor of the Beenstock corn warehouse ... and finds himself facing a legal claim.' Repeated in knowledge check 1 ('in Act 3') and flashcard 1.
findings.truth: The fall happens offstage on the morning of Act 2 and Fred Beenstock reports it; the writ is drafted and produced during Act 2. Act 3 is the wedding party in Will Mossop's cellar, where Hobson is made to settle.
findings.evidence: Project Gutenberg #6347 (1916 Samuel French acting edition of the play), Act II: 'we've a cellar trap in our place that opens in the pavement and your father ... fell into it'; 'Action against Henry Horatio Hobson for trespass on the premises of Jonathan Beenstock & Co., Corn Merchants, of Chapel Street, Salford, with damages to certain corn bags'.

findings.claim: 'A doctor diagnoses Hobson with chronic alcoholism' placed in the Act 3 section; flashcard 4 asks 'What medical diagnosis does the doctor give Hobson in Act 3?'
findings.truth: Doctor MacFarlane examines Hobson in Act 4, a year after Act 3.
findings.evidence: Project Gutenberg #6347 (1916 Samuel French acting edition of the play), Act IV ('It is eight o'clock on a morning a year later'): 'DOCTOR. Chronic alcoholism, if you know that what means ... you've drunk yourself within six months of the grave'.

findings.claim: 'The trespass case against Hobson becomes the mechanism for Maggie's return. Albert Prosser ... is the solicitor handling the case against Hobson.'
findings.truth: The action is Maggie's own invention. She tells Freddy to instruct Albert, and Albert says 'I'm far from saying it's good law, and I'd not be keen on going into court with it', to which Maggie replies 'It won't come into court.' She uses it at the Act 3 wedding party to force a 500 pound out-of-court settlement, 250 pounds each for Alice and Vickey. Maggie's return to Hobson's house is a separate event in Act 4, caused by his illness.
findings.evidence: Project Gutenberg #6347 (1916 Samuel French acting edition of the play), Acts II and III ('the half of five hundred pounds apiece for them to make a start on').

findings.claim: 'Her conditions are clear: ... the name on the sign will change to place Willie's name first.'
findings.truth: The name is Willie's demand, made against Maggie. She says 'I think Hobson and Mossop is best'; he answers 'The best I'll do is this: Mossop and Hobson' and 'Mossop and Hobson or it's Oldfield Road for us, Maggie'. Maggie gives way. Her terms are the half-share and the sleeping partnership.
findings.evidence: Project Gutenberg #6347 (1916 Samuel French acting edition of the play), Act IV.

findings.claim: Willie's literacy work is placed in Act 2 ('By Act 2 ... Maggie insists that he learn to read and write'; practice question 5 says 'Willie's reading lessons in Act 2').
findings.truth: There are no lessons in Act 2. Maggie sets Willie a writing copy on a slate at the very end of Act 3, on their wedding night, and Willie says in Act 4 that Maggie 'set about my education'.
findings.evidence: Project Gutenberg #6347 (1916 Samuel French acting edition of the play), end of Act III: 'Your writing's improving, Will. I'll set you a short copy for to-night ... Great things grow from small.'

findings.claim: 'Willie's inability to read or write' (L3) and 'a timid, illiterate cellar worker' (L5).
findings.truth: Willie can read a little. Asked by Mrs Hepworth whether he can read, he answers 'I do a bit. Only it's such funny print.' What Maggie gives him is writing practice. 'Barely literate' is right; 'illiterate' is not.
findings.evidence: Project Gutenberg #6347 (1916 Samuel French acting edition of the play), Act I.

findings.claim: 'Acts 3 and 4 return to Hobson's shop, but now it is a diminished, failing space.'
findings.truth: Act 3 is set in Will Mossop's own cellar at 39a Oldfield Road, which is the opposite of a return to Hobson's. Only Act 4 goes back to Hobson's, and it is the living-room, described as very dirty.
findings.evidence: Project Gutenberg #6347 (1916 Samuel French acting edition of the play), cast list: 'ACT III. WILL MOSSOP'S Shop. ACT IV. Living-room of HOBSON'S Shop'; Act III stage direction: 'The cellar in Oldfield Road is at once workroom, shop, and living-room.'

findings.claim: 'When Ada Figgins and her mother arrive to defend Ada's claim on Willie ...'
findings.truth: Ada arrives alone, bringing Willie's dinner. Mrs Figgins never appears on stage; Ada only threatens 'I'll set my mother on to you', and Willie admits he is afraid of her.
findings.evidence: Project Gutenberg #6347 (1916 Samuel French acting edition of the play), Act I.

findings.claim: 'But Maggie intercepts: she tells Willie that if Hobson strikes him, they will leave immediately.'
findings.truth: Willie makes the threat, not Maggie. He says 'if you touch me with that belt, I'll take her quick, aye, and stick to her like glue', and after Hobson strikes, 'if Mr. Hobson raises up that strap again ... I'll walk straight out of shop with thee and us two 'ull set up for ourselves.' Maggie's only line in the exchange is 'I'm watching you, my lad.'
findings.evidence: Project Gutenberg #6347 (1916 Samuel French acting edition of the play), Act I.

findings.claim: 'By Act 2, he can declare with evident pride: "I've got my name wrote up on the windows".'
findings.truth: The full line undercuts the pride: 'I've got my name wrote up on the windows, but I dunno so much about being master.' Willie is still diffident here. The clipped quotation is accurate, but the reading of it is not.
findings.evidence: Project Gutenberg #6347 (1916 Samuel French acting edition of the play), Act II.

findings.claim: 'The Married Women's Property Acts of 1870 and 1882 had only recently allowed women to own property in their own name.' Flashcard 9 asks 'Which 1870 and 1882 acts had only recently given women property rights?'
findings.truth: The play is set in 1880, so the 1882 Act had not yet been passed. The 1870 Act let a married woman keep her own earnings; full separate property came with the 1882 Act, two years after the setting.
findings.evidence: Married Women's Property Act 1870 and Married Women's Property Act 1882 (standard legal history); play setting confirmed by the opening stage direction.

findings.claim: 'The 1870 Education Act had introduced compulsory elementary education.' Flashcard 5 asks 'Which 1870 law introduced compulsory elementary education in England?'
findings.truth: The 1870 Forster Act created school boards to fill gaps in provision. Attendance became compulsory under the 1880 Elementary Education Act, which is the year the play is set.
findings.evidence: Elementary Education Act 1870 and Elementary Education Act 1880 (standard educational history).

findings.claim: 'its English premiere at the Apollo Theatre, London, on 24 June 1916' (also in the Key Fact box and flashcard 2).
findings.truth: Sources disagree. The 1916 printed acting edition states 'Its first English production took place on June 22, 1916, at the Apollo Theatre, London.' Wikipedia gives 24 June 1916. Either accept the printed edition and change every instance to 22 June 1916, or drop the day and say 'June 1916'. No exam turns on the day, so this is not edited here.
findings.evidence: Project Gutenberg #6347 (1916 Samuel French acting edition of the play) front matter, vs https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hobson%27s_Choice_(play)

findings.claim: 'overriding his objections and physically removing Ada Figgins'
findings.truth: Maggie opens the shop doors and tells Ada 'you've no business here'. Ada walks out on her own, shouting a threat. There is no physical removal.
findings.evidence: Project Gutenberg #6347 (1916 Samuel French acting edition of the play), Act I.

findings.claim: 'You must refer to the quotation in your answer.'
findings.truth: The spec says each question 'will be preceded by a short quotation from the text, to provide a stimulus for the response'. It is a starting point, not a requirement, and telling students it is compulsory wastes their time.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md line 1122.

findings.claim: 'He stumbles in from the Moonraker's pub, hungover, and lectures his daughters on respectability.'
findings.truth: In Act 1 Hobson enters from the house, hat already on, on his way OUT to the Moonraker's. He has got up late, but the play does not stage him returning drunk in Act 1. He does arrive drunk at the Act 3 wedding party.
findings.evidence: Project Gutenberg #6347 (1916 Samuel French acting edition of the play), Act I: 'HENRY HORATIO HOBSON enters from the house ... His hat is on' / 'Maggie, I'm just going out for a quarter of an hour.'

findings.claim: 'the older, educated woman proposes to the timid, barely literate craftsman'
findings.truth: Willie's stage direction gives his age as 'about thirty'; Maggie is thirty. She is not the older party. The class and education reversals in the sentence are correct.
findings.evidence: Project Gutenberg #6347 (1916 Samuel French acting edition of the play), Act I.

findings.claim: 'Brighouse structures Act 2 so that every scene of Maggie's progress is mirrored by one of Hobson's deterioration' - repeated in the Key Fact box, the takeaways, practice question 2 and flashcard 10.
findings.truth: The play has no scene divisions inside its acts; Act 2 is one continuous scene in Hobson's shop. The contrast between Maggie's rise and Hobson's decline is real, but it is not built from alternating scenes, and a student who writes that in a structure question is wrong about the play's form. Correcting it properly means rewriting a teaching thread that runs through five fields, so it is left for a judgement call: either soften every instance to 'the act sets Maggie's rise against Hobson's decline', or leave it.
findings.evidence: Project Gutenberg #6347 (1916 Samuel French acting edition of the play), Act II is a single continuous scene ('A month later. The shop as Act I.').

summary: Every lesson carries at least one finding. The dominant error is a board mix-up: eleven places across five lessons teach that AO4 rewards analysis of Brighouse's methods, when on this Edexcel section AO4 is written accuracy (8 of 40 marks) and AO2 is not assessed at all - one knowledge check keyed that false answer as correct. Every practice question is labelled 40 marks but marked against a 25-mark band ladder. Lessons 3, 4 and 6 also mislocate three plot events by an act (the trapdoor fall and writ are Act 2, the doctor is Act 4, Willie's writing lessons are Act 3, and Act 3 is set in Will Mossop's cellar, not Hobson's shop). All quotations in the unit check out verbatim against the acting edition.
